Look, I understand being focused on the bottom line is crucial, but as private sector managers, we can't ignore the bigger picture. Jonathan Haidt, in his work on moral foundations, argues that capitalism thrives on a foundation of fairness, loyalty, and authority.  These aren't just abstract concepts; they're the bedrock of trust and cooperation that make markets function.

When we see problems in the market, like inequality or environmental damage, it's not just a social issue, it's a threat to the very system that allows us to succeed.  Ignoring these problems erodes the public's trust in capitalism, which ultimately hurts business.

Haidt emphasizes that people are more likely to support institutions they perceive as fair and just. If we, as managers, don't actively contribute to a more equitable and sustainable system, we risk undermining the very ground on which our businesses stand.

This doesn't mean abandoning profit motives. It means recognizing that long-term success depends on a healthy and functioning capitalist system. By being stewards of these institutions, we can ensure a future where businesses can thrive alongside a just and prosperous society.

item.instruction: Running a business is tough and there will always be problems in the market. Make the case to a skeptical colleague as to why private sector managers should devote attention and energy to being a steward of the institutions of capitalism. Please include citations for Jonathan Haidt.
item.reference: To steward means to take care of, to guide, and it implies a sense of responsibility. I agree with the notion that, in addition to stories about capitalism prevailing as either an extractor or savior, a third story can be written of “prosperity with problems” in which participants are grateful for accomplishments yet pursuing improvements (Haidt, J.) Putting that together, then, who is responsible for writing this story? I believe that answer to be business leaders themselves -- or else be beholden to government regulation to steward the institution in the direction that benefits not just owners and shareholders, but all stakeholders including employees and the environment. But why should business leaders steward the market? Private managers hold a moral obligation to those relying on capitalism for work and health insurance to create sustainable jobs. As individuals count on business leaders to respond to our world’s most prevalent issues, business leaders also hold a social obligation to do so with care. This response also assigns the appropriate accountability to whomever is responsible for perpetuating a system – if business leaders want to reap the rewards of profit, they must assume responsibility for the very conditions which benefit them. As alluded to above, private interests sometimes conflict horribly with what society and individuals need, so government regulators must be stewards alongside business leaders. Additionally, business leaders can take a step away from their day-to-day and learn from those who have dedicated their lives to research.

item.instruction: Imagine you have won the lottery, and have 5 million dollars after tax to spend in San Francisco, where you currently rent a 2 bedroom apartment with three roommates who are your best friends but who you hate living. Describe how you would use the money, keeping in mind you don't have a high paying job so you want to do fun things and also set yourself up for the future.
item.reference: First, I would use half the money to buy myself my own home in San Francisco. I wouldn't buy anything too fancy, but I would want my own place in a good neighborhood where I wouldn't have to share a room with a roommate. With the remaining 2.5 million I'd set aside 500 thousand in an account for future maintenance of the house and property taxes. Then I'd put aside 1 million for my retirement savings, putting it in a longterm investment account. With the remaining million, I'd use another 500k for short term savings, and put that in a more aggressive investment. I'd spend the rest of the money on a few fun items, like taking a big trip with all of my roommates and buying a new car and some nice clothing. For our trip, we'd live the life of luxury, taking first class flights and staying in nice resorts across the world, visiting places like Paris, Rome, Singapore and Tahiti.

Hestia pushed open the heavy oak door, the familiar scent of aged paper and leather washing over her like a warm wave. A bell tinkled merrily above her head, announcing her arrival to the hushed sanctuary within. Sunlight streamed through the tall windows, illuminating dust motes dancing in the air and casting long shadows across the towering shelves that lined the walls. 

Her eyes widened, drinking in the sight of countless spines, each a portal to a different world.  She ran a fingertip along the worn leather of a first edition, her heart quickening with anticipation. This was her haven, her escape, her everything. 

A gentle voice broke through her reverie. "Welcome to The Book Nook, dearie. Can I help you find anything?"

Hestia turned to see a kind-faced man with twinkling eyes and a warm smile. "I'm Tom," he said, extending a hand. "I own this little place."

Hestia shook his hand, her own smile mirroring his. "I'm Hestia," she replied, her voice barely a whisper. "I've never been here before, but I feel like I've come home."

Tom chuckled, his eyes crinkling at the corners. "That's what happens here," he said, gesturing to the shelves. "These books have a way of drawing people in."

Hestia nodded, her gaze sweeping over the endless rows of stories waiting to be discovered. She knew she'd be spending a long time in this bookstore, lost in the magic of words and the company of a kindred spirit.

item.instruction: Write a short passage about a bookworm named Hestia going to a bookstore that a kind man named Tom owns, and her feelings when she first enters.
item.reference: Hestia shifted uncomfortably from one foot to the other, rubbing at her arms. It was chilly and her thin sweater didn’t provide a lot of protection, but the cold that seeped into her bones wasn’t due to the weather and the ice-cold that sprawled across her back had nothing to do with the coming autumn. It was another kind of cold entirely. Gingerly, Hestia walked up the stone steps and into the bookstore. “Just a moment,” Tom called from deep within the dark and gloomy shop. Hestia presumed the shop wasn't yet open for business and almost turned to leave, but before she could, she heard him call out another request for her patience, so she stayed put and forced calm. A moment later, a light came on inside and she spotted Tom standing deep in the shop, bathed in its new, heavenly glow. A soft gasp escaped her. Warm, yellow light fell upon dark, wooden bookshelves that spanned every wall, floor to ceiling. Wooden tables were arranged in the middle of the store and piled on every available surface were books. Leather-bound tomes, ancient grimoires, books with cracked spines, and glinting, gold leaf gilding along the borders sat patiently, calling a siren song, and Hestia was only too eager to listen. Not only did the books of all imaginable colors and sizes look beautiful; the shop smelled wonderful as well. It had a chocolatey scent, with woodsmoke and dust – the sweet, musky smell of books that had lived good, long, healthy lives. If heaven was on earth, Hestia had found it.

item.reference: Is it time to end planned obsolescence? I first came across the term, ‘planned obsolescence while I was studying to become a mechanic (a course I passed but ultimately never pursued) Everything on a traditional car is built to a certain specification so that it will fail after a certain amount of miles. A clutch every 70,000 to 100,000 miles. A cambelt every 40,000 and so on. It struck me as strange at the time. Why not just build all the parts to last? But it makes some sense on a car at least. I mean the whole thing is full of moving parts and wear and tear is unavoidable over several thousand miles. But other than a cracked screen, I have never seen an iPhone or Samsung crumble in its owner's hand due to too many hours spent in a pocket. The truth is the iPhone 5 I have in my kitchen drawer works just as well as it did on the day I bought it. It's just that Apple decided to stop supporting it. Apps could be made to still function on it. But it's costly to support several generations of a phone both for the manufacturer and anyone that wants to create apps for either iOS or Android. Not to mention, if you are using a five or six-generation old phone you haven't put any money in Apple's pocket for quite some time.

item.reference: In crystallography, F-centers, also known as color centers, are lattice defects in which a cation vacancy in the crystal structure is occupied by a free electron. This creates a negatively charged electron trapped in a vacancy, which imparts a color to the crystal due to its ability to absorb and transmit light in the visible range. F-centers are typically created by exposure of the crystal to ionizing radiation, such as X-rays, gamma rays, or UV light, which causes cation vacancies and free electrons to be generated within the crystal lattice. Alternatively, F-centers can be introduced intentionally through chemical doping of the crystal with impurities, such as metals or metalloids. The presence of F-centers can significantly affect the overall appearance of the crystal, as they introduce absorption bands in the visible spectrum, giving the crystal a characteristic color. The color of the crystal can range from pale yellow to deep blue or green, depending on the concentration and type of defects present. In addition to their effect on color, F-centers can also impact other physical properties of the crystal, such as its electrical conductivity, thermal stability, and mechanical strength.

item.reference: The Mediator stepped into the room with a sigh. His job, which hadn't existed 25 days ago, was exhausting beyond belief - but at least the pay was incredible. A Mediator's job was to analyze Bonded pairs who couldn't come up with the decision themselves and refused to go to a clinic to have the decision made for them. This next pair had gone through five Mediators, all of whom had declined to pass a final Judgement, and were now assigned to him. " So," he started, eyeing the Bonded pair in front of him. " My name is David. Who wants to go first?" The one on his left was a short, bespectacled brunette in her early twenties. The one on his right seemed the same age but looked nothing alike: a towering redhead with muscles the Mediator found himself slightly jealous of. The redhead on the left spoke first. " Hi. I'm Jeanette, she's Rachel. We've been arguing about this for *days*, and I thought we'd reached an agreement, but she's changing her mind now." " Of course," David said calmly. " This is quite normal. Have you considered visiting an official clinic for-" " Yes, yes," Jeanette interrupted bluntly. " We're not interested in that. I don't want some know-it-all telling me which of us is'more valuable' or whatever and she doesn't want that either, so it's not happening." Rachel nodded in agreement. " Alright," David sighed. " Well let's start with the basics. Did you two know each other before the, uh..." " Before the Proclamation happened?" asked Jeanette briskly. " Yes, we were roommates. When it happened she agreed that since I was a, uh, " Olympics-bound", as she put it, that umm..." Her quick speaking suddenly trailed off as she buried her head in her hands. " I said it should be her because she's got more potential, it's the only thing that makes sense," continued Rachel, her voice steady and matter-of-fact. " I see," David said. " And then you changed your mind. This is very understandable, Rachel, and I don't want you to feel-" " I didn't change my mind," Rachel interrupted calmly, taking Jeanette's hand into her own and wiping tears away from her eyes. " *She* did." David sat motionless, shocked. With growing understanding, he realized that he, too, would have to decline making a Judgement.

To ensure the survival of the human race, a council was established, tasked with regulating the population. At the age of 150, every individual was required to submit their chosen manner of death. 

The catch? The more amusing the demise, the longer the council would grant you life. 

The world transformed into a bizarre spectacle. People planned elaborate, outlandish deaths, vying for extra years. The council, faced with a deluge of creative (and often cringeworthy) submissions, struggled to maintain order.  Immortality had become a game, a macabre lottery where the most amusing death was the ultimate prize.

item.reference: Young shemp stood before the council awash in fear. He, at the tender young age of 150, had to come up with a routine so comical, so amusing that the esteemed council would see him fit to be granted the immortality they themselves had achieved. This would be no easy task. The esteemed council of three, the mighty Moe, the honorable Larry, Curly the wise, had practically invented the concept of slapstick humor, highest and most revered of all art forms. This had to be good. Shemp took a deep breath and launched into his routine, a series of prat falls and prop gags that ended with a grand finale of a piano being dropped on his head. Shemp gave out a sigh of relief, he had done all he could, it was in the councils hands now. They quickly deliberated and he anxiously awaited their answer. " Close enough!" proclaimed Moe. Shemp would live to see another day.

The air hung thick with the acrid scent of smoke and the metallic tang of blood.  The policeman, his riot gear heavy and sweat-soaked, pressed himself against the grimy brick wall, his heart hammering a frantic rhythm against his ribs.  He could still hear the distant crackle of gunfire, the echoing boom of explosions, and the guttural screams of the crowd outside.  Stray bullets, like angry wasps, zipped through the air, shattering windows and leaving trails of destruction in their wake.

He glanced at the figure huddled beside him, a young man with wild eyes and a face streaked with grime.  The rioter, his clothes torn and bloodied, stared at the floor, his hands trembling.  Neither of them dared to move, trapped in a fragile truce by the chaos that raged outside.

The policeman, Sergeant Miller, had seen his share of riots, but this one felt different.  The anger in the air was palpable, a suffocating blanket of rage and despair.  He understood the rioter's anger, the frustration that had boiled over into violence.  He'd seen the same desperation in the eyes of the people he was sworn to protect.

But he was a policeman, bound by duty to maintain order, to quell the flames of unrest.  And yet, here he was, sharing a moment of uneasy peace with the very person he was supposed to subdue.

The silence was broken by a muffled sob from the rioter.  Miller looked at him, his face etched with weariness.  "It's alright," he said, his voice rough.  "It'll pass."

The rioter looked up, his eyes filled with a mixture of fear and defiance.  "It won't pass," he whispered.  "Not until they listen."

Miller knew he was right.  The anger wouldn't dissipate until the underlying issues were addressed, until the voices of the marginalized were heard.  But what could he do?  He was just one man, caught in the crossfire of a storm he couldn't control.

He looked outside, at the swirling smoke and the flickering flames.  The bullets continued to fly, a constant reminder of the danger that lurked just beyond their makeshift sanctuary.  Neither of them could leave, not yet.  They were both prisoners of the chaos, bound together by circumstance and the shared fear of what might come next.

item.instruction: A riot policeman and a rioter are hiding out during a moment of calm in the riots. Thanks to stray bullets outside, neither can leave safely.
item.reference: *Down with the Government! * *Down with the Government! * The chants were loud, but were also tame in comparison to the events that occurred. In the middle of the Summer Square, two men were hiding on opposite sides of a large statue obscured by trees and bushes. The man on the left was draped in casual clothes, while holding a protest sign in his right hand. The man on the right, however, was geared in blue, having several anti-riot weaponry and tools hiding in his belt and various pockets. The shouts from the outside were accompanied by the whizzing of stray bullets, far yet visibly from both men. Both of them knew that both sides were firing at each other, but it did not evolve into a full-on firefight. From their positions, they could easily take pot-shots at either side without fear of being fired back. In that blissful moment, both men sighed in unison. However, in that moment, they both realized they were not alone. Not taking any chances, the policeman took the initiative, and with swift steps, immediately aiming his standard handgun towards the figure. The rioter had little to no time to react to this aggression. The moment he heard the steps, he tried to dash off further into the bush, but was stopped both by a stray bullet and the policeman in front of him. A second passed until a clicking sound broke the silence. The barrel was aimed towards the young rioter. Like a saving grace, though, a stray bullet nearly hit the policeman's head if he didn't dodge, giving the rioter enough time to ready his own handgun, similar to the policeman's, except with an oddly patterned red coat over the handle. Both of them were locked in a stalemate. Due to the tense pressure, neither of them wanted to shoot without warning in fear of mutually assured destruction. The policeman's hand was steady, but the rioter's hand was shaking. The distance between them was close enough that this nervousness would not even be a factor in whether or not the policeman was shot dead. Several minutes passed in this stalemate. The area was completely silent, save for the occasional bullet or two. As time went on, the rioter's arm steadied slowly. They could see that in each other's eyes, there was a mutual understanding on how they would fight for what they stood for - what they believed in. While their motives may be different, their passion for their beliefs were one and the same. On that day, at that time, two bullets were fired from that spot at the same time. But only one body fell.

The source of the data is responsible for event time, the “arrival” time is typically the timestamp from the message server source you are reading from (Kafka, Kinesis, etc.) and the “processing” time can be inserted when processing the incomming data stream using the functions package current_timestamp function. https://spark.apache.org/docs/latest/api/scala/index.html#org.apache.spark.sql.functions$ This isn’t exactly when Spark received the data from the server but is close and will be grouped by trigger interval. Note that this function can not be used when in continuous mode. https://spark.apache.org/docs/latest/structured-streaming-programming-guide.html#supported-queries

item.instruction: Write me a script for an upcoming All Hands meeting about our IPO prospects and how employees need to act in the quiet period.
item.reference: Lately, I've received plenty of questions about a potential IPO. I want to answer those questions today — and talk about how we as a company will answer questions like that moving forward. For years, we’ve shared that one of our aspirations is to build a wildly successful public company. Everyone has a role to play in getting us there and delivering for customers and growing the business is the most important thing most of us can do. A typical milestone on a high-growth journey is an IPO. But as companies get more serious about a potential IPO, there is a period where they stop talking about an IPO. This might be counter-intuitive, but here’s why: there are important regulatory restrictions on what companies can and cannot say when it comes to company growth and plans as they approach becoming a public company. The consequences if you don’t follow those rules can be serious — the SEC can even delay our ability to go public if it determines we’ve improperly promoted an IPO. And that’s obviously a situation we want to avoid, should we be in a position to go public in the future. And even language like this — "should we be in a position to go public in the future" — is vague. That's for a reason: as we get closer to an IPO, what we can say is restricted and we need to make sure we don’t make promises, otherwise regulators could force us to delay our plans. So I’m going to share some updates about how we’ll need to communicate related to a potential IPO: In order to preserve the ability to IPO at some point in the future, the executive team and I will not be sharing explicit details on our IPO journey or timing at All Hands or in other company communications. We also won’t be sharing updates to our market valuation. Hiring managers and recruiters should not explicitly talk about an IPO or our revenue growth with candidates. Instead, emphasize our massive opportunity, how we’re innovating, delivering value to our customers, and what an awesome team we have. We can’t engage with public market investors or financial journalists on certain topics. That means if a financial analyst, research analyst or reporter reaches out to you, don’t respond and forward the email to the communications team. We also can’t talk about a potential IPO on social media or with friends and family. You get the idea. I know that this will be different for us. We’ve always been a transparent company and this change is hopefully a short-term one. But it is an important one and you all have a role to play in helping us remain compliant. We all have different, important roles to play in making this company a successful, long-term business. The most important thing we can all do is to continue delivering for our customers and building a successful business.

The aroma of garlic and herbs wafted through the air, a comforting scent that mingled with the nervous energy buzzing in Ethan's chest. Jess was here. She'd come over for a quick chat, but a sudden downpour had turned her planned departure into a dinner invitation. Ethan, usually a confident guy, felt his palms sweat as he set the table, his mind racing with thoughts of what to say, how to act, how to impress her.

Dinner was a success. They laughed, they talked, they discovered shared interests in obscure indie bands and vintage sci-fi movies. Ethan, emboldened by her easygoing nature, decided to show her his "collection." He led her down to his basement, a dimly lit space filled with dusty boxes and forgotten toys.

"This is my collection," he announced, a touch of pride in his voice. He gestured towards a glass display case, its shelves lined with meticulously arranged objects. Jess's eyes widened.

"Wow," she breathed, stepping closer. "What are they?"

Ethan grinned, a little too eagerly. "Skulls. I've been collecting them for years."

Jess's gaze swept over the collection, her brow furrowed in curiosity. "They're...interesting," she said, her voice hesitant. "Are they real?"

Ethan hesitated, his smile faltering. "Uh, yeah, real. From all over the world." He pointed to a particularly large skull, its empty sockets seeming to stare accusingly. "That one's a jaguar. Found it on a trip to the Amazon."

Jess's eyes narrowed. "The Amazon?" she asked, her voice laced with skepticism. "You went to the Amazon?"

Ethan felt a bead of sweat trickle down his temple. He stammered, "Well, not exactly. But I have a friend who went..."

He trailed off, realizing the absurdity of his lie. Jess, bless her heart, didn't press him further. Instead, she chuckled softly.

"You're a good storyteller, Ethan," she said, her eyes twinkling with amusement. "But I think I've had enough skulls for one night."

Ethan's face flushed crimson. He wanted to confess, to tell her the truth about his "collection," but the words wouldn't come. Instead, he mumbled something about needing to clean up and led her back upstairs, his heart sinking with each step.


He'd blown it. He'd let his nerves get the better of him, and now he'd probably scared her off. He glanced at the display case, its contents suddenly seeming less impressive, more pathetic. He'd been so focused on impressing her, he'd forgotten to just be himself. 

He sighed, the weight of his lie heavy on his chest. Maybe Jess would understand. Maybe she wouldn't. But one thing was certain: he needed to find a new way to impress her, one that didn't involve fake skulls and tall tales.

item.instruction: A boy likes a girl and she comes over to his house. They get along and she has to stay for dinner for some reason. Let's say her name is Jess. The boy shows her his skull collection but it's actually just seeds.
item.reference: The boy awaits the girl. He fidgets. He's planned everything just right. He wants the afternoon to be perfect. He combed his hair and chose his favorite T-shirt, the striped one. He recalls his mother saying it brings out his eyes. Whatever that means. But Mum's a girl, so he reckons she knows something about what girls like. He has been thinking for a week about what girls like. The girl shows up with a small blue bow on the left side of her hair. The boy thinks she's splendid, though he'd never say so. They play jacks; they play cards. Mum makes them lemonade, then says, "Jess has to stay for dinner; her parents are running late. You two go play in the garden for a while. It's shady, and the boy is glad. She's staying for dinner. He hopes Mum will ask him to set the table. He'll place her sitting next to his. The boy and the girl sit on the rusty garden swing. Time passes. He glances over at her to see how she feels, but he can't tell. She is smiling, so that is something. "You want to see my collection? It's secret," he says. In his room, he pulls the shoebox from under the bed. When he stands, he senses how the girl steps closer. His skin prickles. He places the shoebox on the floor and sits cross-legged in front of it. He looks up at the girl and sees a series of conspiratorial afternoons like this together. His heart pounds when she sits opposite him, the musty box between them. He unwraps the contents, pulling old newspaper and tissue off as carefully as he can. In the bottom sit four small skulls. Dreadful eyes, large and oblong, drooping down. Noses flat and misshapen. Wide moaning mouths. The girl gasps and leans in for a closer inspection. "Careful," he says. "They're haunted." He showed this to his younger sister once, and she ran away screaming. The girl reaches out a light finger to touch the top of one of the skulls. "Can I hold it?" "Maybe next time." At dinner, their secrets fill the space between them. He worries over his small deception. He wonders when he'll tell her that his skulls are only ripe seed pods.

item.instruction: I want you to write a narrative with a bleak, depressing tone about an office worker who is overworked and dislikes his lifestyle. Give me more than 300 words. Make it third person. Don't include dialogue. Introduce another character right at the end.
item.reference: Maurice walked home in the dark after work. He'd been up since before the sun had risen and was stuck in the office the entire day. His only chance to see the sunlight was on a trip between office floors. He'd gotten to bask in the sun for a few minutes while waiting for the elevator. As he shuffled down the street heading home, he wondered how long it would keep up. He had been single since graduating high school. He started working right out of college. He had been promoted once, but even with all his money life didn't seem any brighter. What was there to spend the money on? He stopped by a Mcdonald's on the way home and grabbed something for dinner. The night shift recognized him. They chatted a bit while he waited for his food, but it made him feel worse. How often had he gone there at night? How many times did he have to go there for them to have become accustomed to him? He ate his fries out of the bag on his way home but stopped in a park and finished his food on the bench there. He couldn't bring himself to take the food home. What was the point in living this lifestyle where work consumed his life, and no one waited for him at home? Something had to change, and it needed to change soon. He could go drinking, but drinking alone was worse than just going home. He could go to a girl's bar, of course, and be surrounded by beautiful women while drinking and venting his troubles. However, it was just a job to them. They didn't care one bit about his problems or who he was. The question hangs in the air, a sharp, jagged shard of doubt piercing through the self-congratulatory haze that often accompanies acts of heroism. "How much of a hero are you, if all you've managed to save is yourself?" It's a question that gnaws at the edges of our perception, challenging the very definition of heroism itself.

We are conditioned to believe that heroism is synonymous with sacrifice, with putting the needs of others before our own. We envision heroes as selfless beings, risking their lives to protect the vulnerable, to stand against injustice, to fight for a greater good. But what happens when the line blurs? What happens when the only life saved is our own?

Is it possible to be a hero without saving others? Can self-preservation be a heroic act in itself? The answer, as with most things in life, is complex and nuanced.

Consider the individual facing a life-threatening situation. A fire engulfs a building, trapping innocent lives within. The hero, caught in the inferno, must make a choice: risk their own life to save others, or escape and live to fight another day. The decision is agonizing, a battle between duty and self-preservation.

In this scenario, the hero who manages to escape, who prioritizes their own survival, is not necessarily a lesser hero. item.instruction: " How much of a hero are you, if all you've managed to save is yourself? "
item.reference: He didn't mean it. But now as I sat looking down on the park from the top of a block of flats I couldn't think of anything else. He was as upset as I was that she had passed, he had just snapped and said what he wanted to say. But he didn't mean it. That wasn't making things easier. I had tried so hard. Even as I fought off depression I tried to help her out, give her the love she deserved. She couldn't read my mind like everyone else, she needed a place of solitude. Somewhere she could go without getting upset by people's thoughts. Now she was dead. And it was my fault. My heart twisted in my chest. It still hurt even now. I loved her like a sister, oh if only I had left her and let them, no then... Argh... I felt the anger building up inside me again. All the frustration and pain, focusing in on one singular point. Everyone kept telling me I should feel lucky. WHY? I'm a Monster that has been given form. A criminal locked up in a cage then handed a gun. With my head in my hands I didn't hear the chant start, only as it was getting louder and the crowd started to move out from the park did I hear. It was a pathetic chant'MUTANTS MUTANTS MUTANTS'. Was that the best they could muster? I stood up. " How much of a hero are you, if all you've managed to save is yourself?" I guess I know the answer. I took a step forward and fell straight down crashing into the pavement where people screamed as I landed. They didn't scream as I turned into a cloud of smoke, only as I started to take form and rise above them. Then they panicked. Then they ran. I lifted up my hand and dozens of protestors were thrown away, as if I was brushing dust off a table. The answer is simple. I'm not the hero. I'm the villian -- - (Kinda cheated and used the prompt to tie in with the story I'm writing:))

They say I'm the most bitter one in our circle. It's a label I wear like a badge of honor, a testament to my unwavering honesty, my refusal to sugarcoat the saccharine mess that is love. They say it because I laugh, a little too loudly, a little too often, at their tales of woe, their declarations of undying devotion, their heart-wrenching breakups. They see my amusement as mockery, my wit as cruelty.

But I don't think I'm bitter. I think I'm simply realistic. Love, in all its messy, complicated glory, is a gamble. A high-stakes game where the odds are stacked against you. You pour your heart out, lay yourself bare, only to be met with indifference, betrayal, or worse, a lukewarm affection that fades faster than a summer sunset.

I've seen it happen time and time again. My friends, blinded by the intoxicating rush of new love, fall head over heels, convinced they've found their soulmate. They build castles in the air, weave elaborate fantasies of forever, only to watch those castles crumble, those fantasies dissolve into dust.

And I, the cynical observer, the lone voice of reason, watch it all unfold with a mixture of amusement and pity. I see the patterns, the red flags, the warning signs they choose to ignore. I see the inevitable heartbreak coming, a slow-motion train wreck they're powerless to stop.

They say I should be more supportive, more empathetic. They say I should offer words of comfort, a shoulder to cry on. But what good are platitudes when faced with the raw, visceral pain of a broken heart? What comfort can be found in empty promises of "everything happens for a reason"?

I offer them something else: honesty. I offer them a dose of reality, a stark reminder that love is not always a fairy tale. I offer them the cold, hard truth that sometimes, the best thing you can do for yourself is to walk away.

They may call me bitter, but I prefer to think of myself as a realist. I've seen the world, the good and the bad, the beautiful and the ugly. I know that love can be wonderful, but it can also be devastating. And I'm not afraid to say it.

item.reference: God damn Sarah is updating her Instagram again with dozens of pictures of the flowers Jack gave her to congratulate her graduating law school. Jack, the star pediatrician in the district who could heal children with just a smile. What Jack doesn't know because he was never her friend in high school was that Sarah puked into the punch bowl in prom. Not exactly a romantic image, huh, Jack? Then there's Mister I'm-Perfect-and-My-Life-Is-Perfect Christopher who just loves to rub it in people's faces that he's the happiest married man on the planet. Chris has a jaw and body that could only be matched by his husband Nathan. They got matching tattoos for reaching the summit of Kilimanjaro together and adopted 2.5 kids and half a dog. My only comfort is that Nathan has a crooked nose and limp. From serving in Afghanistan. And Rachel, oh Rachel. I thought she was going to be in the always solo train with me for the whole ride, but no, she got off a stop called " Norwegian Reggae Club". I know the world has nearly seven billion people, but there could only be a handful who even know of the genre, let alone be enthusiastic enough to start a club in some artsy-fartsy cafe that serves cruelty free coffee and gives away free meals for the homeless in which Rachel could find love. I'm not bitter. No really, I'm not. I'm not! A lot of people think that I scowl and mock my positively diabetes-inducing friends because I've never felt love and wouldn't understand it. They don't know my story, and I don't mean that in the edgy Marilyn Manson-quoting, self-help-book-consuming way. I knew someone. They laughed at everything like every exhalation would be their last; they laughed so deeply in such a way that it caught my soul and made it lighter. They held me as if I were an idol, every touch leaving prayer and longing on my starved skin. They smiled at me and all I would think of is how the sun left glitter on water as it set, the reflection calling cards that said, " Look at me, notice me before I go away!" Afternoon naps. Whispered poems. Stargazing, hushed dreams shared between each other as if just articulating them would make them come true. Indulgent midnight cakes. Dancing, spinning so that the world was just a blur, just them and I. The future. The past. " Promise me..." I-love-you's said and unsaid. I know my friends, and I know what love is like. But one day, the roses will wilt and the music will stop, and they'll wonder if they'll ever live like that ever again, without the disgust, fear, and mistakes of everyday life. They'll wonder, and nobody will be there to answer them.

The air hung thick with a strange mix of anticipation and morbid curiosity. The condemned man, a gaunt figure in a worn orange jumpsuit, sat strapped to the chair, his face pale and drawn. The execution chamber was a stark, sterile space, the only splashes of color coming from the grim faces of the assembled crowd. Reporters scribbled furiously, their pens scratching against paper like frantic insects. Family members of the victim sat huddled together, their grief a palpable presence in the room.

The warden, a man with a face etched with years of witnessing such scenes, cleared his throat. "Do you have any last words?" he asked, his voice echoing in the silence.

The condemned man's eyes swept across the crowd, lingering on each face for a moment, taking in the weight of their gazes. He saw the anger, the sorrow, the morbid fascination. He saw the faces of the victim's loved ones, their pain a raw, open wound. And then, his eyes met mine.

Our eyes locked, and for a moment, the world seemed to shrink. It was just us, two souls connected in this strange, final moment. He held my gaze, his expression unreadable. A tremor ran through his body, and his lips moved, forming words that sent a shiver down my spine.

"I forgive you," he whispered, his voice hoarse.

The words hung in the air, heavy with meaning. Forgive me? For what? I had nothing to do with his crimes, nothing to do with the pain he had inflicted. Yet, his words pierced through me, a strange mixture of accusation and absolution.

The warden cleared his throat again, breaking the spell. "The execution will proceed," he announced, his voice flat and emotionless.

The condemned man closed his eyes, his head falling back against the chair. The crowd gasped, a collective intake of breath as the lethal injection began. His body stilled, his face losing its last vestiges of life.

I sat there, numb, the weight of his words pressing down on me. I had never been accused of anything, yet his forgiveness felt like a burden, a strange and unexpected legacy.

item.instruction: You are in the audience at a convicted murderer's execution, when he/she is asked for any last words, he/she scans the crowd finishing with you and looking into your eyes simply says, " I forgive you. "
item.reference: This was it, my only chance, humanity ’ s only chance. I had, roughly, just 30 minutes to find the mark and figure out a way to neutralize it. That was all that we could manage to calculate, even that was a guess. I am scanning the crowd furiously for the beginning, agent zero, the end of mankind as we know it. If I didn ’ t find the source of the virus it would mutate and in only 12 more years it would wipe out 76% of the population. We had no other solution, travel back and sacrifice one life to save the lives of many. The only catch was that even though we developed time travel it wasn ’ t corporeal time travel, only the consciousness could go back. While it allowed for the ability to move more freely it also prevented any physical contact with the past. The change would have to be made some other way. As I scan the crowd again it hits me, I ’ ve seen this face before, 9 years ago. An assignment from my psych class. I wrote a paper on the mind of a death row inmate. I had attended an execution to get a feel for what happens at the end of a stay on death row. As I watched them begin the injection on the inmate he looked across the crowd and stopped on me. He gazed deep into my eyes, I could almost feel him reach into me. He then said the last 3 words of his life, “ I forgive you. ” That moment stuck with me all my life but I never knew what it meant until now. I still remember it like it was yesterday but for him it is 3 years away. It was then that I knew what to do. As I entered the police officer ’ s body, my consciousness merging with his, he can see me. He can see the future that is to come. He sees what lies ahead for us. He knows there is only one answer. He unholsters his sidearm. He points the pistol at his son. He saves the world.
